other.about: The rule-based weather block (track W; weather design): circulation regimes, what condenses, climate averages for slow physics, formations by rule and drawn storm systems behind one swappable contract.

circulation.source: Hadley edge from Held and Hou 1980 (small-angle form, phi_H = (5/3 g H dh / (Omega a)^2)^1/2); cells from the Rhines arrest wavenumber k = (beta/2U)^1/2 (Rhines 1975); trends checked against Kaspi and Showman 2015. Wind scale, contrast, tropopause depth and the rain profile weights are tuned to Earth (docs/fudges.md).

supply.source: Energy-limited precipitation: the latent heat flux, a share of the sunlight reaching wet ground, falls back as liquid (Pierrehumbert 2010, ch. 9 energy budget). Sunlight reaching the ground falls with air column, fitted to Earth, Venus and Titan; cloud cover from latent flux fitted to Earth (docs/fudges.md).

rules.because: Too little air for cloud or wind: no weather.
No surface under the air: belts and zones between alternating jets, storms and polar features (W3).
One face to the star: rising air and a permanent cloud shield under the star, clearer night side (Yang, Cowan and Abbot 2013; Showman and Polvani 2011).
Air too thin for weather to organise into belts: thin ice cloud, frost, fog in basins and dust storms where there is dust (Zurek and Martin 1993).
Slow spin lets one overturning cell reach the pole in each hemisphere: weak jets and a broad cloud band (Held and Hou 1980; Kaspi and Showman 2015).
Fast spin breaks each hemisphere into many narrow belts and jets (Rhines 1975; Kaspi and Showman 2015).
Moderate spin: a tropical cell, a mid-latitude storm track and a polar cell in each hemisphere.

cyclones.source: Storm-track cyclones as baroclinic waves (Eady 1949; Chang, Lee and Swanson 2002): wavelength 3.9 N H / f; life, wind and winter boost are Earth-like stand-ins (docs/fudges.md)

tropical.source: Genesis over sea above 26 °C and at least 5° from the equator (Emanuel 2003, after Palmén 1948); yearly count, life and size are Earth-like stand-ins (docs/fudges.md)

dust.source: Planet-encircling dust storms come in some years, in the southern spring and summer near perihelion (Zurek and Martin 1993); chance and depth are stand-ins (docs/fudges.md)

orography.source: Rain from forced uplift on windward slopes and a rain shadow behind (Roe 2005); the uplift coefficient is a stand-in (docs/fudges.md)

lightning.source: Flash rate from cloud-top height, continental and marine (Price and Rind 1992); storm density is a stand-in (docs/fudges.md)

bands.source: Same jets and band edges as the surface pack's S6 cloud deck (base-surface regime_features.clouds): jets = round(sqrt(a Omega / U)) from the Rhines scale (Rhines 1975), U about 150 m/s on gas giants and 400 m/s on ice giants (below 50 Earth masses), 2 x jets bands with edges evenly spaced in sin(latitude), retrograde jets half the prograde. Zones (anticyclonic shear) and belts (cyclonic) alternate from an equatorial zone, so prograde jets sit on the poleward edge of zones (Vasavada and Showman 2005). Gas giants superrotate at the equator; ice giants have one broad retrograde equatorial jet and prograde jets at high latitude (Vasavada and Showman 2005; Smith et al. 1989). Equatorial speed factors are a cartoon (docs/fudges.md).

stratification.source: Deformation radius L_d = N H / f (f = 2 Omega at the pole), H the pressure scale height at 1 bar. One Brunt-Vaisala frequency N for every giant, fitted so Saturn's polar Burger number (L_d / a)^2 is 1.6e-3, the Saturn-regime value quoted by Brueshaber and Sayanagi 2021 (docs/fudges.md).

polar.source: The Burger number Bu = (L_d / a)^2 is the parameter that decides a giant's polar regime: lowering it goes from one polar cyclone (Saturn-like) to many circumpolar cyclones (Jupiter-like), and the forcing energy hardly changes that (Brueshaber, Sayanagi and Dowling 2019). O'Neill, Emanuel and Flierl 2015: a / L_d <= 30 gives one strong polar cyclone, >= 40 many vortices (so Bu <= 6.25e-4 ring, Bu >= 1.111e-3 single, between drawn), and weak convective forcing gives a diffuse pole with no polar cyclone (internal heat below 0.1 W/m2 here). Diffuse cap from Bu >= 4e-3, the geometric mean of the Saturn-regime 1.6e-3 and ice-giant 1e-2 values quoted by Brueshaber and Sayanagi 2021. Ring counts 5 to 9 around Juno's 8 (north) and 5 (south) (Adriani et al. 2018). Cyclone sizes in deformation radii and the ring gap fitted to Jupiter's north ring; polar jet 0.8 of the wind scale (docs/fudges.md).

polar_jet.source: The circumpolar jet sits one polar Rhines length from the pole: on the polar gamma-plane f = 2 Omega (1 - r^2 / 2a^2) the Rhines arrest gives L = (U a^2 / 2 Omega)^(1/3) (kernel derivation from Rhines 1975, docs/fudges.md). Saturn: 78.6 degrees, against the hexagon's about 78 degrees N (Godfrey 1988).

polygon.source: Rule fitted to Saturn's hexagon at about 78 degrees N (Godfrey 1988). A strong, narrow circumpolar jet settles into a stable meander whose number of sides is set by the deformation radius against the jet (laboratory wavenumber 6: Barbosa Aguiar et al. 2010; numerical 3 to 8 sides with jet width, strength and curvature: Morales-Juberias et al. 2015). Here: a polygon only on a coherent circumpolar jet (single polar vortex regime), at or above 70 degrees, of at least 100 m/s, and narrow enough that its latitude circle holds 3 to 8 waves; sides n = round(2 pi r_jet / (k L_d)), clamped 3 to 8, with k fitted so Saturn gives 6 (docs/fudges.md).

ovals.because: a great oval, a long-lived anticyclone in a zone, where the shear between the neighbouring jets turns the same way as the storm
ovals.source: Great ovals live in the anticyclonic shear zones between jets and drift with the local wind (Vasavada and Showman 2005). Rate and life (log-uniform 10 to 300 years) tuned so a Jupiter-like giant usually carries one or two, like the Great Red Spot and Oval BA (docs/fudges.md).

strings.because: a string of small ovals, anticyclones lined up along one zone like Jupiter's String of Pearls
strings.source: Strings of small anticyclonic ovals form along zones (Vasavada and Showman 2005); rate, life and spacing tuned (docs/fudges.md).

dark_spots.because: a dark spot, an anticyclone on an ice giant that clears the high methane cloud so the deeper, darker air shows, with bright companion clouds on its poleward side
dark_spots.source: Neptune's Great Dark Spot, an anticyclone near 22 degrees S about 13000 km across with bright companion clouds (Smith et al. 1989); such spots last years. Rate (0.2 a year) and life (log-uniform 1 to 6 years) tuned (docs/fudges.md).

outbreaks.because: a planet-circling outbreak: on a cooler gas giant moist convection is held back for years, then breaks out as a great white spot whose tail wraps the planet
outbreaks.source: Saturn's Great White Spots, giant convective storms about every 30 years (about once per Saturn year) whose disturbance encircled the planet within weeks (Sanchez-Lavega et al. 2011). Here: gas giants colder than 150 K at 1 bar, one chance per orbit; the temperature cut, chance, duration, size and encircling time are tuned to Saturn's 2010 storm (docs/fudges.md).

clouds.source: Cloud classes by temperature after Sudarsky et al. 2000 (as the S6 cloud deck); zones carry thick high cloud, belts thin high cloud that shows the layers below; covers and optical depths are stand-ins (docs/fudges.md).
